transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-14 09:30 PDT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Claire (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Stratus Head of ML), Rafael (Cloud Architect), Marta (Security Ops)

Summary (auto): quick discovery on private VPC deployment, networking constraints, security and pilot next steps.

[00:00] Claire Huang: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Claire from Redwood, and with me is Diego, our solutions engineer. How's it going?
[00:12] Priya Nair: Morning, yeah thanks. We, uh, excited to talk through private deployment options. We've got some pretty tight requirements around networking and keys.
[00:25] Diego Alvarez: Hi all. Quick agenda—confirm constraints, dig into networking (peering vs endpoints), region and latency, security (KMS, SOC2), and agree next steps.
[00:38] Rafael Ortiz: Sounds good. To start, we cannot have a public endpoint. All inference traffic must come from our VPCs, no public IPs, and we need customer-managed KMS keys for encryption at rest.
[00:52] Marta Kline: And audit logs that we can ingest into our SIEM, plus SSO/SAML integration. HIPAA controls apply to some datasets.
[01:05] Claire Huang: Totally understood. Redwood Private supports private endpoints and VPC-only deployments; we can run inside your VPC or peer, depending on model. Diego, do you want to walk through the network options?
[01:18] Diego Alvarez: Sure. High level—we offer two common patterns: 1) Interface endpoints/private ENIs + PrivateLink from Redwood control plane, where the data path stays private and you never need public IPs; 2) VPC peering or Transit Gateway connections if you want direct peering between Redwood and your VPCs. If customers have Direct Connect or Transit Gateway already, that can be used to centralize traffic.
[01:44] Priya Nair: Which is more recommend for strict environments? We've got multiple accounts in us-west-2 and a central transit.
[01:53] Diego Alvarez: For strict no-public-IP, PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is usually simpler because you create interface endpoints in your subnets and traffic goes to Redwood's private endpoint. If you already use Transit Gateway, peering via Transit Gateway is fine but has extra routing complexity. Also, note that PrivateLink only supports certain services and requires ENIs in subnets.
[02:12] Rafael Ortiz: What about VPC CIDR sizes, NATs, and egress? Our subnets are /24s for each availability zone. Will we need additional IPs?
[02:23] Diego Alvarez: Yes, interface endpoints consume IPs in the subnet; for medium scale you may want /23 or ensure there are free addresses. For heavy throughput, we recommend dedicated subnets for endpoints and enabling ENI scaling. If using peering/Transit, you avoid endpoint IP consumption but need route propagation and possibly NAT gateways for outbound traffic.
[02:45] Marta Kline: We also have strict egress controls; all outbound traffic must traverse our proxy and be logged. Can Redwood work with proxy egress or require specific NAT setup?
[02:58] Claire Huang: We can support customer egress via NAT as long as callbacks from Redwood to the model runtime are routed through the private path. For some variants we may need outbound to our control plane — Diego?
[03:10] Diego Alvarez: Yes, the control plane requires connectivity to coordinate model versions, metrics, and billing; however in Private deployments we can run a local control plane inside your VPC or in a private-managed control plane connected over a private link. We have options: fully customer-managed control plane (on-prem/VPC) or Redwood-managed but private linkage.
[03:30] Priya Nair: Ideally we want the control plane inside our VPC or at least on a private peered network. We cannot have metadata leaving to public internet.
[03:38] Diego Alvarez: Understood. We have a Private offering that can place the control plane in your VPC. There are tradeoffs—Redwood-managed private CP shortens setup time, but customer-managed gives you full network isolation.
[03:52] Rafael Ortiz: Regarding regions—our primary workloads are in us-west-2 because of data residency and latency to users. Is Redwood available in us-west-2?
[04:03] Claire Huang: Yes, we support deployments in us-west-2, us-east-1, and eu-west-1 for Private. For other regions we can discuss lead times.
[04:12] Priya Nair: Latency SLOs—what can we expect for 256-token responses on p99? We need under 500ms for some real-time features.
[04:23] Diego Alvarez: Depends on model and instance type. For quantized LLMs on GPU-optimized instances in the same AZ, p95 can be sub-100ms for short responses; p99 for longer or larger context can approach a few hundred ms. For strict 500ms p99 at 256 tokens, we usually advise dedicated capacity with pinned GPUs and KV cache warmups. We'll run benchmarks with your prompt set.
[04:49] Priya Nair: Okay, we'll send a representative prompt set.
[04:54] Claire Huang: Great. On security, Marta, you mentioned KMS. We support customer-managed keys (CMK) in AWS KMS for encryption at rest. You can supply a CMK and we integrate via IAM roles. Any specific key rotation or HSM requirements?
[05:09] Marta Kline: HSM-backed CMKs are preferred; rotation policy must be in line with our controls and we need to ensure Redwood doesn't have key access. Also need proof of key usage in audit logs.
[05:22] Diego Alvarez: That's fine. We integrate with AWS KMS using roles and never persist the unencrypted keys. We can provide CloudTrail logs and we also emit audit events which you can forward to your SIEM. We'll include a sample CloudTrail mapping in the playbook.
[05:37] Rafael Ortiz: About authentication—SSO, SAML, SCIM for user provisioning?
[05:44] Claire Huang: Yes, Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning in the console. For private deployments, we can connect to your IdP over private network as well.
[05:55] Priya Nair: How about model updates and rollouts? We need to control versions and approvals.
[06:01] Diego Alvarez: You can pin model versions, control rollouts with canaries, and Redwood's console shows per-model metrics. For private stacks we can disable automatic updates—everything is versioned and you approve rollouts.
[06:14] Priya Nair: Good. Any compliance documents you can share?
[06:18] Claire Huang: We'll send SOC2 Type II, HIPAA overview, and our security whitepaper.
[06:23] Marta Kline: Network diagram would be helpful. Also, examples for Terraform/CloudFormation to create interface endpoints and route tables.
[06:32] Diego Alvarez: We'll include Terraform snippets and a sample architecture: endpoints in private subnets, route tables, security groups allowing only our ENIs, and optional Transit Gateway example.
[06:45] Rafael Ortiz: One concern: we have multiple accounts and a central egress account — will Redwood's endpoints support cross-account interface endpoints?
[06:54] Diego Alvarez: Yes, interface endpoints can be created in each account, or you can centralize using peering or Transit Gateway. We also support AWS PrivateLink across accounts with endpoint services. We'll detail the recommended pattern for multi-account.
[07:10] Priya Nair: For pilot sizing—we plan for 50 rps with average 120 tokens per request and peak bursting to 200 rps. Any guidance?
[07:21] Diego Alvarez: That helps. We'll map that to GPU types and concurrency. Likely a mix of multi-GPU instances and batching optimizations. For predictable latency, Dedicated reserved capacity is recommended. We'll propose a pilot cluster for those numbers.
[07:38] Claire Huang: Next steps then: Diego will prepare a network playbook and diagram; I'll send SOC2 and pricing; Priya will share the prompt set and traffic profile.
[07:47] Marta Kline: Timeline-wise we want to get security sign-off within 2-3 weeks and start a pilot in 6-8 weeks if everything checks out.
[07:56] Claire Huang: That aligns with our typical private pilot. We'll aim to have the technical deep dive next week with your infra team. Diego, are you available for Wednesday?
[08:06] Diego Alvarez: Yes, Wednesday 10am PT works. I'll bring our infra notes.
[08:12] Rafael Ortiz: One more operational question — do you support VPC flow logs and can we ingest detailed call-level logs?
[08:20] Diego Alvarez: We emit audit events and request-level logs; for privacy-sensitive workloads we pseudonymize identifiers, but we can push logs to your S3 or CloudWatch via private endpoints. VPC flow logs are independent and will capture ENI-level flows.
[08:35] Priya Nair: Good. On billing, how does usage attribution work across accounts? We need org-level cost breakdowns.
[08:42] Claire Huang: We support tagging and org-level reporting; for dedicated/private we can attach to your billing account or provide detailed invoices. We'll include sample billing output.
[08:52] Marta Kline: Are there any blockers for HIPAA BAAs?
[08:57] Claire Huang: We support BAAs for Private deployments; legal needs to sign standard BAA, and we'll include that in the contract sketch.
[09:06] Priya Nair: Perfect. One thing—do you have experience with on-prem GPU clusters (air-gapped)? We may want that eventually.
[09:13] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we have an on-prem appliance path. It's a longer lead time, requires more integration, but it's supported. We'll scope that separately if you choose it.
[09:25] Rafael Ortiz: Ok, thanks.
[09:27] Claire Huang: Great—recap of action items and I'll follow up with calendar invites. Thanks everyone.

Meeting end.
